concepts.name: Algorithm as step-by-step procedure
concepts.summary: State that an algorithm is a finite, unambiguous sequence of steps that transforms input into output and solves a defined problem.

concepts.name: Linear search
concepts.summary: Explain how checking each element in turn finds a target and why it may need to inspect every element.

concepts.name: Binary search on sorted data
concepts.summary: Explain how repeatedly halving a sorted range locates a target and why sortedness is required.

concepts.name: Counting steps as input grows
concepts.summary: Describe how the number of basic operations grows with input size rather than measuring seconds on one machine.

concepts.name: Simple sorting by comparison
concepts.summary: Explain how a simple sort such as selection or insertion sort orders a list by comparing and moving elements.

concepts.name: Recursion as self-reference
concepts.summary: Explain that a recursive function solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller instance until a base case stops it.

misconceptions.text: Binary search works on any list as long as you pick the middle element.
A faster-running program on my computer always means a better algorithm.
A recursive function does not need a base case because it stops when the work is done.

concepts.name: Big O notation for growth rates
concepts.summary: Express the running time of simple loops and code as O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n) or O(n²) by dropping constants and lower-order terms.

concepts.name: Tracing recursive calls
concepts.summary: Trace recursive calls and returns, including the call stack, for functions like factorial and Fibonacci.

concepts.name: Mergesort
concepts.summary: Apply the split, recursively sort and merge steps to sort a list in O(n log n) time.

concepts.name: Quicksort and partitioning
concepts.summary: Apply pivot selection and partitioning to sort a list recursively and recognise its typical and worst-case behaviour.

concepts.name: Iterative binary search implementation
concepts.summary: Implement binary search correctly with proper bounds and midpoint updates, avoiding off-by-one errors.

concepts.name: Breadth-first and depth-first traversal
concepts.summary: Apply BFS with a queue and DFS with a stack or recursion to visit all nodes of a graph or tree, tracking visited nodes.

misconceptions.text: Big O gives the exact running time, so an O(n) algorithm is always faster than an O(n²) one.
Quicksort is always O(n log n).
Graph traversal does not need a visited set because graphs have no repeated nodes.

concepts.name: Recurrence relations and Master theorem
concepts.summary: Write the recurrence for a divide-and-conquer algorithm and solve it to derive its running time.

concepts.name: Best, worst and average case
concepts.summary: Analyse how input shape changes running time and distinguish worst-case from average or expected behaviour.

concepts.name: Divide and conquer design
concepts.summary: Decompose a problem into independent subproblems, solve them recursively and combine results, as in closest pair or maximum subarray.

concepts.name: Greedy choice strategy
concepts.summary: Build a solution by repeatedly taking the locally best choice, as in interval scheduling or Huffman coding.

concepts.name: Dynamic programming with overlapping subproblems
concepts.summary: Solve problems like Fibonacci, knapsack and longest common subsequence by defining states and reusing stored subresults via memoization or tabulation.

concepts.name: Graph representation and traversal cost
concepts.summary: Compare adjacency lists and matrices and derive the O(V+E) cost of BFS and DFS.

concepts.name: Dijkstra's shortest path algorithm
concepts.summary: Compute shortest paths from a source in a graph with non-negative weights using a priority queue and edge relaxation.

misconceptions.text: Dynamic programming is just recursion with a different name and gives no speedup.
A greedy choice that looks best locally always yields the optimal solution.
Dijkstra's algorithm works correctly with negative edge weights.

concepts.name: Proving greedy correctness
concepts.summary: Evaluate whether a greedy strategy is optimal using exchange arguments or greedy-stays-ahead proofs and find counterexamples when it is not.

concepts.name: Optimal substructure and DP formulation
concepts.summary: Identify optimal substructure, define state and transitions, and choose an evaluation order including space optimization.

concepts.name: Amortized analysis
concepts.summary: Analyse the average cost per operation over a sequence, as with dynamic array doubling.

concepts.name: Shortest paths with negative weights
concepts.summary: Choose among Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford, DAG relaxation and Floyd-Warshall based on weights, cycles and query type.

concepts.name: Sorting lower bound
concepts.summary: Explain the decision-tree argument that comparison sorts need Ω(n log n) and when linear-time non-comparison sorts apply.

concepts.name: Randomized quicksort analysis
concepts.summary: Evaluate how random pivot choice yields expected O(n log n) and compare pivot strategies.

concepts.name: Graph algorithm selection
concepts.summary: Select and justify algorithms such as topological sort, Kruskal, Prim, or BFS versus Dijkstra for a given graph problem.

misconceptions.text: Amortized cost is the same as average-case cost over random inputs.
Any sorting algorithm can beat O(n log n) with clever comparisons.
If a problem has optimal substructure, greedy will solve it.

concepts.name: NP-completeness and reductions
concepts.summary: Evaluate problem hardness by reducing known NP-complete problems to it and decide when exact algorithms are infeasible.

concepts.name: Approximation algorithms
concepts.summary: Judge approximation algorithms by their provable ratio, as for vertex cover or metric TSP.

concepts.name: Designing novel algorithms from structure
concepts.summary: Create new algorithms by modelling a problem as a graph, DP or divide-and-conquer structure and proving correctness and complexity.

concepts.name: Cache and real-world performance
concepts.summary: Evaluate how constants, cache locality and hybrid designs like introsort or Timsort make asymptotically equal algorithms differ in practice.

concepts.name: Advanced analysis techniques
concepts.summary: Apply and critique advanced tools such as potential functions, probabilistic analysis and smoothed analysis to bound running time.

concepts.name: Network flow and matching
concepts.summary: Create reductions of problems like assignment and cuts to maximum flow and analyse the resulting algorithms.

concepts.name: Randomized and parallel algorithm design
concepts.summary: Design randomized or parallel algorithms, specifying error probability or work and span tradeoffs.

misconceptions.text: NP-complete means a problem cannot be solved, so it is pointless to try.
Asymptotically faster algorithms always win in practice.
Randomized algorithms are unreliable because they may return wrong answers.
